html:
The first two warrior governments of Japan, which ruled in the emperor's name from 1185 to 1573. The emperor and court stayed in Kyoto, but real power lay with the shogun, the military commander, and his vassals.

Kamakura (1185 to 1333). Minamoto no Yoritomo won the Genpei War against the Taira clan and set up his government at Kamakura, in the east. He placed military governors and land stewards across the country. After his line died out, the Hojo family ruled as regents for the shogun. The shogunate beat back the court in the Jokyu War of 1221 and survived the Mongol invasions of 1274 and 1281, helped by storms later called kamikaze, divine winds. The cost of the defence, with no land to reward the warriors, weakened it. Emperor Go-Daigo overthrew the Hojo in 1333.

Muromachi (1336 to 1573). Ashikaga Takauji turned on Go-Daigo and founded a new shogunate in the Muromachi district of Kyoto. Rival imperial courts, north and south, fought until 1392. The Ashikaga shoguns sponsored a high culture:

  • Zen monasteries and ink painting
  • Noh theatre
  • The golden pavilion of Kinkaku-ji

Ashikaga power was always weak. The Onin War of 1467 to 1477 wrecked Kyoto and began the Warring States period, a century of fighting between local warlords. Oda Nobunaga drove the last Ashikaga shogun out of Kyoto in 1573, and unification under the Tokugawa followed.
sum: The first two warrior governments of Japan, which ruled in the emperor's name from 1185 to 1573. The emperor and court stayed in Kyoto, but real power lay with the shogun, the military commander, and his vassals.
